candidate.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — elimination, assistive devices, wound/skin care and comfort
candidate.educational_objective: Apply the cited evidence to recognize the uniquely safest or most accurate nursing response in the clinical situation tested by V2-Q0142.

options.A: Limit fiber and fluids so bowel movements occur less often, reducing the number of times cardiovascular stress can occur during defecation.
options.B: Use the prescribed bowel regimen and avoid straining or prolonged Valsalva-like effort because it can produce marked hemodynamic changes during defecation.
options.C: Stop all stool-softening therapy once bowel movements become less frequent because constipation is preferable to medication use after myocardial infarction.
options.D: Use repeated forceful bearing down to shorten each bowel movement because brief high-pressure straining places less stress on the circulation.

candidate.rationale: Straining during defecation produces Valsalva-like hemodynamic changes and can provoke substantial blood-pressure and heart-rate shifts. In a client with cardiovascular disease, preventing constipation and minimizing forceful straining is safer than repeated bearing down.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Review evidence describes straining at stool as a Valsalva-like maneuver that can raise blood pressure and trigger cardiovascular events in susceptible patients.
candidate.source_document_title: Constipation-induced pressor effects as triggers for cardiovascular events
candidate.source_locator: Ishiyama et al., J Clin Hypertens. 2019;21:421–425, PMID 30761728 — abstract/review: straining at stool causes BP rise and may trigger cardiovascular events
candidate.stem: A client recovering from a myocardial infarction has chronic constipation and reports needing to strain during bowel movements. Which teaching is most appropriate?
